title: The DiCecco Daily "Training Camp Legends Series:" Catching Up With Former Eagles WR/KR Jeremy Bloom
text: [music] Hello and welcome in to another episode of DCO Daily. It's Andrew Deeco here, Eagles beat reporter for insidethebirds.com and it's a special edition because I'm joined by 2006 fifth round pick of the Philadelphia Eagles, number 147 overall. That would be one wide receiver Jeremy Bloom who's kind enough to carve out a few minutes and take a walk down memory lane with me. Jeremy, how you doing? >> Doing great, Andrew. Good to see you. >> Good to see you. So, we have a lot to cover in a short amount of time, but I feel it's really important to go back to your two seasons at Colorado. You only played two years there and I understand that it had to do with an NCAA rolling. Could you explain that a little bit? Yeah, I so I you know entered the University of Colorado as a freshman and coming off the heels of uh my first Olympics um and being the number one ranked skier in the world. So that created a bit of a hiccup for the NCAA because I was compensated through endorsement money and of course that was not allowed in the NCAA back then. So they basically said you got to pick between football and skiing. Uh and if you want to play football here, you can't have any endorsement uh for your ski career, which um obviously didn't work out too well for me [laughter] in that. >> So in 2006, you participated in the Winter Olympics. How there was a big gap there from your football playing time. >> How did you stay in shape and how did you prepare for the NFL draft? Well, so you know, I I decided to to forego all my sponsorships. So, I got to play my freshman and sophomore year at the University of Colorado. And then I was sort of broke, you know, and and I wanted to fund a campaign to get back to my second Olympics in skiing, which would would been Torino in 2006. And so, when I accepted the endorsements, the NCAA um declared me ineligible for my junior and senior season. So, I really just I focused on skiing um exclusively during those two years. And that next year I I ended up winning more World Cups than consecutive World Cups than anybody in in the history of sports. So it was working and I was so, you know, sort of focused on skiing. Um, hindsight being 2020, I I wish I would have done more football exercises during those two years because when I got drafted to the Eagles and went to a very pass happy Andy Reid offense and a training camp that was pretty brutal, man, like you are sprinting all day every day. And, you know, my body just wasn't conditioned for that. That's the reason I tore my hamstring my my rookie season uh in Philly. But, you know, look, it it it all worked out in the end. And um but yeah, that that was the reason for that gap. >> So, you alluded to this, but let's get right to it. Your first training camp, what were your initial impressions? Was it everything that you expected or was a little bit more intense? >> I mean, it was a pinch me moment on every level if I'm being honest. It's like, you know, I've I always dreamed about playing in the NFL and, you know, 5 foot n 170 lb guys don't typically make it there and and so just to be in the locker room with Donovan McNav and Brian Dawkins and Brian Westbrook and just an incredibly talented team, it was the year after Tio left with his famous sit-ups in the in the uh driveway. [laughter] But no, but it was it was incredible. and to be coached by Andy Reid, who's, you know, if not the best coach ever, certainly top top three. Uh, and to be immersed into a city that I had deep family connections to. My my dad grew up in Villanova and went to Lower Marian High School and um so, you know, it was just a it was a dream come true on on on every level and um certainly taught me if I didn't know otherwise what hard work was. Those training camps at at Lehi were uh as hard of, you know, the some of the hardest things I've ever done before. Um but yeah, I mean, you know, it was it was incredible time in in Philly. Obviously, I wish I would have had more success on the field, and I wish I could have figured out a way to stay healthy. Um on one hand, but on the other hand, um I'm sort of glad I only last three three years in the NFL. Those guys are big and and fasted. like I I kind of like thank my lucky stars at this phase of life that I didn't have a long career. >> Now, you mentioned your father, Larry. He is from Villanova, Pennsylvania. Did he brief you at all on what to expect from the Philadelphia fan base? >> He did. And and I can tell you I had no idea uh going into it what what what it was truly like being from Colorado. Um but uh you know you you you've never met you know a more passionate group of people about a team and and that's a great thing. Um and it can play out in spectacular ways if you're winning and it can be pretty disastrous if if if you're lose if you're losing. >> What are your takeaways from Lehi? It's a storyried pastime. A lot of you you'll hear a lot of people talk about the old days when the Eagles would go to Lehi. What what were your takeaways from that? I mean, two a day practices, you know, like like they used to be with with uh you know, not a lot of thinking about the players, you know, health and and all that type of stuff. They they really were brutal. And, you know, I think I'm fairly qualified to say that, you know, being an Olympic athlete in an entirely different sport and, you know, understanding what hard work is required to be the best in the world. Um, uh, yeah, they they were brutal, man. Uh, especially, I think, for receivers because you were literally I mean, you're you're pushing your body to the max. you're 100% all day every day, you know, running and and putting a lot of toll on on your body. So, look, I think, you know, um the memories from Lehi weren't that pleasant if I'm being if I'm being open, just because it was it was tough. Uh and it was very competitive, very hot, very humid. Um but I will say it was it was awesome to see the fans show up in Lehi. Like every day at practice, we had thousands of passionate fans literally cheering us on, which was cool. Now, also in your draft class was Jason Avant. Was were you guys roommates uh during your time at Lehi? >> We weren't roommates, but we were very close friends. U you know, love Jayvon and, you know, was was uh just so happy for him the amount of success that that he had uh and and what he did to contribute to to Eagles Nation. But uh yeah, Hank Basket was in that class if if you remember Hank and >> uh Omar Gaither and you know bunch of other uh you know guys that um it was fun. It was a fun class to be part of. >> Now I'm sure Andy sort of cowers his approach to every player. What was his approach with you and and to that extent wide receivers coach David Cully? >> Cully. I love Cully. Cully's a character man. I honestly I spent way more time with Cully than than Coach Reed and I never really felt like I got to know Coach Reed um that well and and that's probably true for I think for most players. He I would describe him a bit more introverted than extroverted and having been able to play for Mike Tomlin um who's very extroverted and and Andy Reid who I think is much more introverted. I don't know man I didn't really get a chance to to know him. He he wouldn't say much during team meetings. Then you spend a lot of time with your coordinators. Marty morningwig was uh my OC when when I was there and and Cully and uh just a great great group. But you know Mike Tomlin just sort of seeing the difference between Andy Reid and Mike. I mean you know he was much more um outgoing and outspoken and and more of that team leader in a in in a locker room than um than Coach Reed was. >> Going into the summer uh of 2006. I'm not sure if you were aware of this, but there was a a lot of buzz surrounding you. Did you feel that when you got to training camp? >> Um, you know, I I did feel it. I was, you know, coming off a good campaign at the Olympics and, you know, being a three-time world champion and, you know, two-time Olympic skier, I I understood what that would entail, but I I really tried to do my best to keep a low profile because it's tough to be a rookie on a team and, you know, you really want to earn your stripes, not not inherit them, you know, coming coming in. Um, but you know, when I was put on IR because I, you know, tore my hamstring, I I worked incredibly hard that that off season and and had a great mini camp, was coming into training camp, you know, really really with a lot of momentum. Um, and, you know, unfortunately, you know, suffered another injury. Uh, broke my toe against the Ravens in that preseason game. And at that point, hamstring torn, broken toe. Like, it just wasn't meant to be, man. And that's that's sort of what I was how I was feeling and thinking and you know grateful for the Steelers to give me another opportunity but for whatever reason um just couldn't couldn't stay healthy. >> Not not to revisit it but do you remember how you tore your hamstring that summer? >> Oh yeah I definitely do. was at the end of practice returning a kickoff and you know body really tired you know and and again like hadn't played football in two two years muscle muscles weren't really conditioned for those long practices and I was just returning a kickoff and I went to go make a move make a cut and I just felt that thing like go immediately and I just fell to the ground and you know I had never had a a hamstring injury and you know the problem with hamstring injuries is you never know when you're healthy so you always I always went back to practice too early. Like, oh yeah, it feels good. Feels good. And then you'd sprint, you'd turn it on and it would go again and it would go again. And this probably happened, gosh, I want to say five or six times. And it's unfortunately one of those injuries, especially if you're a speed guy, you sort of have to put it on the shelf. If I would have done anything differently, I would have shelfd it like for, you know, that whole off season. Um, I just would have shelfd it and got healthy. But, uh, it's it's a tricky injury to navigate. Now, you already came into training camp having competed at the highest level, but I understand that football is unique. Did you feel any kind of pressure even internally going into your first camp? >> Well, I mean, you always feel pressure in the N it's it's the NFL. Like, if you're not feeling pressure, I you know, I better check your heartbeat. Um, you know, it's got to be one of the most, if not the most competitive leagues in the world. I mean, there's only 52 guys on a roster. What, 3,000 guys across the league? And you have tens of millions of people, kids all around this country trying, you know, the best athletes in this country play football. I mean, there's been a lot of commentary about the World Cup soccer. I mean, you're seeing that kid from from Norway excel. He's basically a middle linebacker and he'd probably be an average middle linebacker. Like, if you took all the DBs and the receivers and the middle linebackers, you took the hours in their life that they played football and you put them into soccer, we dominate. like it wouldn't even be fun to watch the World Cup in my opinion because I think the US would dominate that. So, the NFL is so incredibly competitive and you look at the college sort of feeding ground for for talent coming up through the draft and yeah, you feel a ton of pressure and you see that revolving door. I mean, you'll go into your locker room on a Tuesday and your buddy next to you, the locker totally cleaned out and he's gone. You didn't even know it. like it's just you sort of realize that pretty quickly that it is a revolving door and you got to do you got to show up well uh in meetings and on the field and and and all the things if you're going to remain in the league >> because your background is so unique. Did you get a lot of questions from teammates with regard to skiing and things like that? Did you get any ribbing from teammates? >> Yeah, you always get ribbing for for sure, especially when you're, you know, on covers of magazines and things like that. But um I I I would say there's this common mutual respect amongst most athletes and Olympians. Like a lot of athletes just wish they they could be an Olympic athlete. It's cool to represent your country. And so I think most of the question is like, man, what was it like to be an Olympian and all that stuff and it's cool to now see flag football coming as an Olympic sport in in LA. And it'll be interesting to see are there any current or former NFL players that actually play on those teams. I'm curious to hear your perspective on this, Jeremy. In retrospect, do you feel in any way that your skiing background took away some mobility on the football field when you were going through >> Yeah, I know for sure. Like mentally, I felt like the two helped each other because I never had a mental offseason. I was competing in skiing through the winter and then I was right there in training camp. So, I never had an offseason mentally, which I thought was helpful. Physically, they're two incredibly different sports. I mean, there's a reason there's only one person that's ever skied in the Olympics and played in the NFL. Like, and and it's it's it's, you know, it's it's incredibly um a unique expo sport if you think about it this way. Like, in football, especially for a receiver, you need a ton of ankle flexibility and strength to be able to make people miss and get in and out of breaks and cuts and things like that. And in skiing, you're essentially putting a cast on your ankle, which does not help for flexibility or strength. A ski boot is essentially a tight cast. And so, you know, there's a lot of things that um I think I would have gained if I was a one sport athlete, if all I did was play football or all I did was was ski. And I think there's a there's a good case to be made that I would have been better um at that sport if that's all I did. But in all cander and transparency and honesty, I wouldn't trade the experiences that I had with both for being the Michael Jordan of basketball or the Tom Brady of football. To me, that was really less important than getting to experience a team sport at the highest level, getting to experience an individual sport at the highest level. Of course, I had, you know, more success on the global stage in skiing than I than I did obviously in in football. But those relationships, those experiences, I wouldn't have trade those traded those. And I'm just really grateful that I was able to experience the highest level in both those sports. >> At what point did you decide you were done with football and you were going to move on to the next phase of your life? >> It was in It was definitely in Pittsburgh when when I was released for the second time in three years. I had an opportunity to go to the practice squad in Tampa Bay and I'm coming off a, you know, torn hamstring, a broken toe. And besides that, a pretty, you know, enjoyable experience. And I always told myself that I was never going to be one of those athletes that just stuck around. And when my time had come, like it was going to be my time and I'm going to go climb a new mountain. And I just determined at that point it's it's no, I'm not going to go to a practice squad. You know, I think all signs and signals are saying to move on with your life and go try something different. And so I I listened to those voices and I left and I got into tech and started an enterprise software company of all things. I didn't even know how to code. Uh and it was an incredible 10-year journey, you know, building and growing that company ultimately to exit the the company was acquired in 2021 by a private equity firm out of Boston. Uh but yeah, it was it was another fun journey very similar to sports. just dive into the deep end, sink or sink or swim and a bit of a game of survival and uh but yeah, it was fun to sort of, you know, sharpen my teeth in a totally different area. >> Hey, Philly fans, game day is stressful enough. Parking, traffic, long lines, we've all been there, but when it comes to your cannabis, Camden Apothecary makes it easy. This is the dispensary for sports fans. Just minutes outside of Philly, with plenty of free parking, you'll be in and out fast. No hassle, no waiting. And they don't just care about convenience. Camden Apothecary is all about the guest experience. Their staff makes sure you feel taken care of every time you walk in. Plus, they carry only the best quality cannabis at the fairest prices. So whether you're stocking up for the tailgate, the watch party, or celebrating a big win, you know you're getting the good stuff without overpaying. They even show love to the community with specials for fans, students, service members, and healthc care pros. Camden Apothecary, top quality cannabis, great prices, and an experience made for Philly fans 21 and up. >> You kind of alluded to it earlier in our conversation, Jeremy, but what was your welcome to the NFL moment? >> Getting hit over the middle uh against I guess it was the Ravens in my first preseason game. Um, you know, the biggest difference between returning a punt in college and returning a punt in the NFL is not necessarily the speed guys, the DBs, the lighter guy. Like, they're all quick in big time college football. It's the linemen. It's the linebackers. It's the defensive ends. They are so much faster and more nimble and quick and and smart than you find in college. I mean, I would watch I was with Broadri Bunkley uh who I think was the first round draft pick in my draft class. Huge guy like Florida State. I mean, he did the agility ladder like like a linebacker in in in uh in college or a DB in college. And those guys are so fast and so nimble and they it really hurts when they hit you. So, getting hit by one of those big guys that was meaningfully faster than anybody I'd ever seen in college was definitely like, "You sure you want to stay in this le? You you sure this is what you want to do for a living? [laughter] >> Now you after football went into a lot of really interesting ventures. And if I'm correct on this, you were a DJ at MTV. [laughter] >> That was actually before football. That was like MTV beach house days. That was after my first Olympics. I wasn't a DJ. I was what's called a VJ. uh which is like a host like a Carson daily for you know one of their beach house shows which was which was just just pure fun and you know didn't take that one too seriously. >> And were you also on a dating show is that right? Yeah, it was called The Choice. Um, which turns out to be a bad choice for me to say yes to, but [laughter] it was like if you've ever seen that uh the the show um The Voice where you're like not looking at the the musician and you can turn your chair if you like what you're hear you hear. The same uh producer that created that show created the choice and you would date somebody by just hearing and asking them questions and then you turn the chair and see what they actually look like. Uh but again that was like lighthearted fun you know didn't really take that one too serious and at a phase of my life when I was single so said why not go have some fun on the show. >> How does one even become a a contestant for that? >> I don't know they reached out to me and said hey we think you'd be a good fit. Are you interested? And said I said sure I got some time. >> Well let's bring it current because what you're doing right now I think is very fascinating. I would love to hear a little bit more about it. You're a CEO of the X Games. How do what led you to that path and could you talk a little bit about what that job entails? >> Yeah, I mean definitely, you know, sports led me to this job. I I was a freestyle mogul skier which is very adjacent to the X Games action sports and so I know from an athlete perspective what it takes and then as I mentioned when I left sports I I started an enterprise software company. So I sort of understood after building that company for 10 years what it takes to create value and build a successful product and a successful company. Um and then you know after selling that company tox it was a nine figure exit. So it was a great exit for the team and and and working inside of private equity for three years as a CEO. I was hired to to run the XG games and the the XG games is owned by private equity now MSP sports capital which owned the McLaren F1 team and a big part of the Phoenix Suns and a bunch of pro soccer teams. a really great group of people who understand how to drive value in sports. And so, yeah, I was I was hired about a year and a half ago to build a league inside of action sports. The first league ever inside of action sports. It's called the Moon Pax Games League, and it's four different teams in the summer, four different teams in in the winter. Uh all these teams are individually owned. So, we we sold all these teams. They went through a draft. Five men, five women. Um S. Paulo, Tokyo, New York, and LA are the summer summer squads. We're in the mix of our season right now. season stop three is in a couple weeks in New Orleans where we'll we'll crown the the first ever league champion and hand over a check for a half a million bucks. But it's going great, man. Like it's it's getting adopted. We're putting big ratings on TV shows. In fact, the Aspen X Games was the most rated highly rated TV TV show at the X Games in in in seven years. Um, and you know, we're feeling really good about, you know, building uh building action sports back up to be bigger than they ever have been before. And obviously it pulls at my heartstrings because I I love these sports. You know, it's uh skiing and snowboarding in the winter and skateboarding and BMX and moto in the summer. So, it's a it's a fun gig. >> Now, that seems like quite an undertaking. How do you even go about establishing a team? What are the early stages of that? She was like the number two at the WNBA, reporting directly to Kathy, the commissioner. And I tasked Annie with building out the operating system for our league. Everything from how do free agencies work, how does free agency work, how does the draft work, how do contracts, all these types of things. And she she's done a really, you know, great job inside of the league office building the framework for that league. Um, but then you you sort of have to surround yourself with great talent. Brought in a CMO from Nike and Beats by Dre. Brought in a head of revenue from the World Surf League and previous, you know, before that ESPN and and and NBC. So, just really build out a a good core team around the business. Um, and around this league to go build it out. Um, and I think it's the, you know, probably the biggest reason why why we're having such early success. >> You mentioned New Orleans. Do you also have Tokyo on the horizon? Is that coming up? >> Yeah, we just finished Tokyo. So, I just got back from Japan a couple days ago and um that that event went went great just outside of Tokyo in a town called Cheba. >> Uh we had thousands of people show up and put we'll put that on ESPN and ABC this weekend. Uh but uh another great event and you know in Sacramento our kickoff we we broke an attendance record of 52,000 people went through the gates. That was the most highly attended X Games uh postcoid. So um yeah, we're feeling good making progress. and and where can those listening and watching find out more information on that? >> Yeah, xgame um xgames.com is a great place to to learn about the league and follow the athletes and of course all of our events are on the networks of ESPN and ABC which will be uh on on TV this weekend with Japan and then live in New Orleans uh at the end of the month. >> That's awesome, man. What a story. What what a story. And uh Jeremy, I appreciate you carving out some time and talking about everything. And man, it's really exciting what you're what you're doing right now. >> Thank you, Andrew. Really appreciated my time um as part of Eagles Nation. Wish I could have contributed to the the success of the team a bit more uh for the fans. But, you know, I I always look back at at that moment very fondly, and it's been, you know, just an honor to to be able to wear the green and and represent the birds. So, go Eagles. I'm a lifelong fan now, obviously, and cheer for the team and appreciate you having me on. >> Absolutely. Well, that's going to do it for this episode of DCO Daily. For Jeremy Bloom, I'm Andrew Deco and I'll catch you all on the next one. >> [music]

title: 49ers Insider Grant Cohn's Honest Assessment of Boston, Massachusetts
text: Anyway, I just got back from Boston. I was there for a week and a half. I have takes if you guys are interested. Never been to Boston before. Actually once I went with my dad in 2020 2012 for a weekend. The Niners played the Patriots. Uh won that game. Tom Brady, Colin Kaepernick, Aaron Hernandez. Remember that? I was there for two nights. In terms of scale, it's a lot like San Francisco. It's about 50 square miles, about 700,000 people. it's very pretty where it's pretty. Uh I was staying in Jamaica Plain, which was right next to Jamaica Pond, which was part of the Emerald Necklace. I mean every few every neighborhood, there's this beautiful park. And they have these things in Boston called they they call they have lakes. Well, at least what I would think is a lake. Like in Oakland, we have Lake Temescal and Lake Merritt. And you got Lake Berryessa and Lake Tahoe. But no, no, no. In in Boston, they're all ponds. Which is such a quaint little British word. And I guess I look at what's the difference between a pond and a lake. Apparently a pond is supposed to be shallower so that think like, you know, water lilies and stuff can grow on. Whatever. So there's ponds and stuff. And ponds are quaint. I think it's very quaint. And what's funny is I was staying in Jamaica Plain and we would um go into downtown, you know, go to like Orange Theory and stuff. And he'd look at the phone and be like, "20 minutes to drive, 20 minutes to take a train, 20 minutes to bike." It's one of these very old towns that's not built for cars whatsoever. So just biked around the town most of the time. That was pretty fun. Not a lot of hills. Uh what else did I like about Fenway was cool. I would have been really I would have liked to actually go to a game in Fenway, but they were out of town the entire time I was there. But I was going to Orange Street like right right around it, so I got to feel for the neighborhood. It's pretty close to downtown. It's got a whole it is a whole economy around it. It's a cool neighborhood. It seemed like a fun place to watch a baseball game. Also, this is I got this hat there, the Tasty Burger. It's their most famous burger in Boston. It was solid. Here are my Do I have gripes? I have gripes cuz I I liked it a lot. But I'm just chauvinistic about the Bay Area. And I just don't I'd rather live in the Bay. Like Boston has good food, but we have better food. And like what they're really known for is, you know, seafood. For sure, great seafood. We have good seafood, too. Like I went over and had the lobster rolls, delicious, loved them. We have good lobster rolls, too. So, I don't know. I don't know. And they have like a lot of Mexican food in Boston, which blew my mind cuz it's like why? None of it's good. Why Why? I mean, it's okay. It's a ton of it. They have good Italian food. They have good cannolis. Uh good good Asian food, good Thai, good Chinese. But every time they have something nice, I'm like, "Yeah, we got that." We we just call it a lake, you call it a pond. I went to Cape Cod for a few days beautiful, man, beautiful. Reminded me of Sea Ranch. You know, just a couple hours up Highway 1 in uh on the California coast. Beautiful. title: Cincinnati Bengals Wide Receiver Analysis | Steve Smith's WR Room Series
text: The Cincinnati Bengals, Steve, we do believe they might have the best one-two punch at the receiver position in the NFL, but where does the entire room stack up? Well, we're going to break it all down right here. It is a room, Steve, that is extremely top-heavy. We'll start with the guy that most people believe is the best receiver in football. [music] The most recent triple crown winner joins your elite illustrious club when he did that a couple of years ago in Ja'Marr Chase. Can Ja'Marr Chase, and this is what everybody's just worried about, I think he might have, not worried about, but just curious about. He has maybe the highest floor, but also the highest ceiling of any guy at the receiver position in the NFL. How does he go to another level? Or we're so used to just the dominant performances, what else would you want to see him at? >> I just want to see Ja'Marr Chase really just be comfortable. >> Mhm. >> Right? Comfortable in his own skin in regards of not pressing, but also understanding that there are going to be times, well, we've seen where there is Joe Burrow or is Joe Flacco at the quarterback position that he doesn't have to be the answer to everything. And that's one of the biggest things that has been holding back the Cincinnati Bengals. They rely so heavily on the pass and just throwing the football all over the lot, right? With a bad offensive line and no ability to really run the football on a consistent basis. They believe in passing the ball and everything. And I know I'm it's shocking to hear a wide receiver say that, but you do got to give your guys some kind of advantage of not being predictable. So, the Cincinnati Bengals are very complicated team because I love seeing the ball thrown all over the lot. But I do believe that Zac Taylor is on the hot seat. I'm talking about hot seat. title: PFT PM Mailbag: Questions surrounding first-year head coaches | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: From Bill. Which first year AFC coach of the two gets the most of his generational quarterback and team, coach Joe Brady or coach Jesse Minter? I think a lot of it depends upon the competition in the division. And Jesse Minter's in a division where there are three new head coaches. The Ravens are favored to win the division for whatever that means. The Bills are dealing with a team that just went to the Super Bowl. Oh, and that we haven't really noticed it because there have been other storylines that have been consuming the coverage of the New England Patriots, but the Patriots have gone out and addressed some of their weaknesses and they're trying to get better. I think there's more pressure on Brady. But there's also a greater degree of continuity with Brady. He was the offensive coordinator. Now he's the head coach. Offense, I don't want to say it's fine. There are flaws in the personnel, which I think contributed to the firing of coach Sean McDermott, even though and this gets back to the whole talent versus coaching, but there are still flaws in the personnel that they've tried to address by, among other things, trading for DJ Moore. So, there's continuity, there's familiarity, but there's is a higher bar for the Bills. New stadium. And this whole coaching change was about punching through to a Super Bowl. I know they only got to the divisional round last year, but this team wants to get back to a Super Bowl for the first time since the 1993 season. And anything less than what they did last year, overtime of a divisional round game, is going to be a clear failure. In Baltimore, it was just time. At least that was the team's position. It was time. The relationship after 18 years with John Harbaugh had run its course. It was time for a change. They didn't go far from the Harbaugh tree to get Minter. They went to the Harbaugh tree. They hired Jim's defensive coordinator for crying out loud. There's still some new to go with the old, but this team didn't make the playoffs last year. So, if you just get to the playoffs, it's an improvement over what happened last year. So, look, I would say my initial thought when I saw this question was to say Brady. I think that it'll probably be Minter because if we look at this as who gets the most out of the quarterback and the team, well, who best exceeds the expectations? The expectations are higher for the Bills than they are for the Ravens. Minter and the Ravens are in a better position. And so far, it seems like Lamar Jackson's all in with what they're doing. I think there's a chance it's going to be Minter because he's stepping into a situation is less precarious, with a lower bar, and without the extra focus and attention and scrutiny. It was just an odd situation in Buffalo. Something was clearly wrong, and the decision was made not just to fire the coach, but to promote the GM, and to promote the offensive coordinator. And there's some language in there that makes it clear the judge is not happy with the NFL's efforts to delay this thing as long as possible. And that's the key. In my opinion, they don't want Flores, Horton, and Wilks to be able to start pursuing the truth. They don't want them to be able to start sending to the lawyers representing the NFL and the various teams what we call a notice of deposition for the owner of the Dolphins, Stephen Ross, the owner of every team that's been sued, the commissioner. That's when it gets interesting. I've said this before many times. When you get folks who are accustomed to submitting to no authority other than their own, and you get them in a setting where they are expected to answer questions, pointed, direct, blunt, aggressive, sometimes when the circumstances call for it, hostile questions. They get pissed. And it comes out. We had gotten and I can't remember how I got my hands on it. I can't remember whether it was reported somewhere, somehow we got a copy of the transcript of the deposition that the commissioner gave in the still lingering insurance dispute over the massive concussion settlement. when you read a transcript of a deposition, it gets very dry very quickly. You got to know when to skim, you got to know when to slow down, you got to know what you're looking for. And it's just words on a page, but there were multiple instances where I could tell he wasn't happy with whatever question had been asked. And that's one of the ways that you get good stuff. The thinking is if you can legitimately frustrate and agitate the witness there's a chance the truth is going to trickle out accidentally. There's another approach, too, where you can make the witness ridiculously comfortable and act like you're the witness's best friend. And through that thing that you can create a vibe where it's a conversation the truth can also spill out that way. I'm not saying anyone goes in to commit perjury in these settings. The reality is people have locked into their version of the events. Here's why this happened. Here's why we did what we did. When it's time to go testify you're not going to suddenly do a 180 and say, "Well, that was just the version we came up with. That's why those cases were so hard. That's why I don't miss it cuz those are the cases I handled. To prosecute a case like that as the lawyer representing the plaintiff, it is a lot of work because you have a lot of people who are sticking to the party line. And you have to come up with ways to get through that. And then you have to come up with arguments that the facts don't make sense. That if you did what you did for the reason you did it, when you consider other relevant factors, it doesn't hold up. It's not logical. It's hard to do. Very hard to do. The NFL's been trying to delay that. Because one of the reasons they have this in-house arbitration process is they want to keep this stuff secret. They don't want to have someone like me get my hands on Michael Bidwill's 6-hour deposition in the portion of the case that relates to Steve Wilks and some of the allegations that we know he's already made. As it relates to things that happened while Steve Keim, the former GM, was suspended for some period of time at the start of the 2018 training camp. The burner phone issue, remember that? From the Terry McDonough arbitration. So, they want to keep this process of discovery deferred for as long as possible. The problem with pushing it too far. You don't want to piss off the judge. Not that the judge is going to overtly hold it against you. There is so much discretion on so many issues that come to the attention of a judge during the handling of a case from start to finish. And the judge can go either way. You don't want the judge to be thinking that you deserve to have all of these things go against you. You don't want the judge to be upset with you. There's a lot of walking on eggshells that happens in any given case, especially when you're in a smaller jurisdiction and you're going to practice in front of the same judge over and over again. Now, I don't think that is as much of a concern. This should be more about Hey, this is the judge who's going to be making rulings in this case until the case is over. And the judge isn't happy. And we haven't even gotten this thing started. So, maybe it'll finally get started. And maybe we'll start to see and hear some of the things that go on at these depositions. And maybe Brian Flores, Steve Wilks, and Ray Horton will move toward the day where we go to court and we let it all play out and we let a jury decide. A jury that is completely disconnected from either party in this case, any of the various teams and plaintiffs. They can decide. The way it should be. That's the way it should be. That's why this chronic effort to rig the process, and I know we live in an age where a lot of things are accused of being rigged. This is a rigged process that the NFL has been using. How can you not call it rigged? I've said many times, why would you even want to be in a position when you're the commissioner to be the one to decide this case? Why do you want to be in this spot where doing the right thing means pissing off the people who decide whether or not you're going to keep the job? one of these days I think, or as I mentioned in the PFT post, one of these years, this thing will move forward and there'll be a trial, unless there's a settlement. And that's the last point before I move on. I've been asked when this case has come up in radio interviews or just conversations, there've been questions from folks that were submitted to this podcast. Has the NFL tried to settle this? Will the NFL try to settle it? My guess would be the NFL has made no effort to settle the case because they believe they can force the whole thing to arbitration and the case has a very different value if it's going to be in arbitration than if it's going to be in open court. And now, here we are. We know we're going to go to open court. The NFL has exhausted, I believe, all reasonable efforts to get it to arbitration. This would be a time for the NFL to make the plaintiffs an offer they can't refuse. And that's where it gets interesting. Because what if Brian Flores' mindset is I don't want your money. I want justice. I want my day in court because it's not just for me. It's for everybody else that didn't get a fair shot at either getting a job as an NFL head coach or keeping a job as an NFL head coach. So, go ahead. Keep offering. I'm going to keep saying no because this is what I want. Now, there's a certain number and I don't know what it is, but there's a number between $100,000 and a billion dollars. There's a number somewhere in there you say, "Well, well, let me rethink my position. this would be an opportunity for the NFL to try to write a really big check and not have to do all this stuff. That not only could set the stage for a bad day in court, but they got to think about the PR side of this. There's going to be a lot of meat that becomes available to people who cover the NFL and who are inclined to pay attention to it and to talk about it and to publicize it. We'll see where it goes. Hi, it's Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. Hit subscribe for the latest news and analysis from Profootballtalk.

title: 'I was amazed': Mike Florio on Argentina's comeback vs England | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: This may be other than what I'll be saying on Monday, the 20th of July, the day after the FIFA World Cup championship game. This will probably be the last time I talk about it unless there's something very interesting that busts through the NFL bubble. The semi-final match from Wednesday, Argentina defeating England 2 to 1. Most of these games I've been able to watch live or close to live. Like, maybe I'm 15 minutes behind and then at half-time I can catch up with the live action. Yesterday was a challenge. Yesterday I had radio in Pittsburgh on 93.7 The Fan at 3:30 p.m. Eastern, half hour into the match. I had other stuff going on, phone calls and haircut and got my workout in early cuz I knew the late afternoon was going to be packed with things that I had to take care of and I wouldn't be able to watch it. So, the way that it worked out, I was able to start watching it at 5:00, but I knew that at 6:10 p.m. Eastern, 3:10 p.m. Seattle time, I was going to do my weekly spot on radio out there on KJR. And I knew that the first thing they'd talk about is whatever happened between Argentina and England. So, I spent most of the 70 minutes from 5:00 to 6:10 clicking the 15-second button because I've gotten to the point where I can tell what the next 15 seconds is going to be. I know whether I need to stop and watch because something good may happen or I can just click click click my way through. And I got it done just in time for the call to come. Finished the game just in time for the call to come, and I was amazed. I assumed England had it in the bag. I saw them weather the storm down a man against Mexico clinging to a one-goal lead in Mexico City. They weathered the storm. They went into the shell and they just stoned Mexico's attack until the referee blew the whistle. Whenever the referee feels like getting around to blowing the whistle, and I kind of love that part. We're so used to knowing exactly when something ends, the last second, the last out. A walk-off, whatever. But to just have this vague idea of, well, it's Is it Is he going to Is he going to blow Is he going to blow the When's When's he going to When's he going to blow the damn whistle? one thing I liked about what happened is I think that there are certain things that are universal to competition. Regardless of what the sport is. And I know that there's been a lot of criticism of England's coach for going into a defensive posture up one nothing. And I don't necessarily have a problem with that because they were in that same posture for an extended period of time against Mexico, and they had one fewer guy, and it worked. It worked. But here's the problem. And this is the thing that I think is true in any sport where you have offense and defense. Once you have settled into the defensive mindset and then all of a sudden, the game is tied. I think it's hard to flip the switch. And I think the temptation, particularly in soccer in that moment, is to say, "Let's just get through to the 30 minutes of extra time." But, when you're the team that was down, and you're getting closer and closer to the end of the game, you tie it up then. Number one, you're already in offense mode. You don't have to flip a switch. And number two, you can be a little looser. We were done. All right. Let's go. Let's just keep rolling. We got nothing to lose here. And if England should happen to score a goal, all right, we're exactly where we were before we scored the goal that tied the thing up. So, I just think that psychology is applicable and transferable from sport to sport to sport, to anything you do that's competitive where they keep score. What is your mindset? What attitude have you settled into? And when circumstances dramatically change, how hard will it be to change your attitude? Change your mindset. And this is all happening on the fly, in the middle of the crucible. One of the commentators from Fox made that point. I think it was Thierry Henry. When you're in it, it's different than when you're watching it. Same thing applies in football. That game moves fast. And the decisions have to be made quickly. And there isn't an opportunity to have the same kind of detached analysis that you can have when all you're doing is monitoring the situation for things that are interesting and things you can analyze based on your own experience and knowledge and skill and whatever. it's a lot easier to say what someone else should decide to do than to make a good clear-headed decision in that moment to ignore the time pressure and make a good decision. That's why Bill Belichick is arguably the greatest game day coach in any sport ever. Now, there may be other flaws, especially later in his career when it comes to some of the decisions he made, roster management, development of young players. I think one of the reasons that they never developed the young receiver who was drafted any higher than round seven is because they just didn't show the patience necessary to give that guy a chance to become what he could be. And the misguided decisions with how to run the offense after Josh McDaniels left to become coach of the Raiders, that contributed to the downfall, but game day coming up with a plan for game day and executing the plan. It's one thing to come up with the plan, you have to execute it and you have to make some decisions And you're the one making them and you're the one everyone is looking to to make them and that can be a challenge. So, I thought that element of it was very, very interesting because it was relatable to other sports and I highly encourage you to watch Sunday Spain and Argentina for the World Cup final. They're also doing a third-place game. I had forgotten they do a third-place game. You know, I think they did a playoff bowl in the NFL years ago where they had like a third-place game and they stopped doing that. Could you imagine that the two teams that lose in the AFC and NFC Championship games would get together for one more completely meaningless game? That would never happen now. I can't believe they ever did it. Okay. Hi, it's Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. Hit subscribe for the latest news and analysis from Pro Football Talk.

title: 2-time World Cup champion Ali Krieger on the NWSL and the World Cup | Women’s Sports Now
text: It's time to talk about some soccer, everybody, with our next guest who knows what it takes to win at the highest level. She's a two-time World Cup champion, an Olympic medalist, an NWSL champion, and now one of the great soccer analysts at ESPN. Let's welcome in Ali Krieger to the show. Ali, >> [laughter] >> welcome, welcome. Thanks for coming by. >> Hi, thank you so much for having me. I'm so pumped to be here. How are you? >> I'm great. Better now that you're here. Let's talk a little bit though about Queens last night because more than 42,000 fans showed up at City Field. That broke the record for a women's sporting event in New York. It was the rematch of the championship final between Gotham and Spirit. I mean, this was an iconic night, and you didn't just watch history. You had a seat inside of it. What did City Field sound and feel like? >> Yeah, it was unbelievable. It is such an achievement and such a historic moment for NWSL, but also for Gotham. I you know, it's it's tough that we always have to go to a baseball stadium and play in the stadium in order to get 42,000 fans without, you know, just just asking for that in our own stadium. But outside of that, it's it just is bringing more people and making them aware that we even have a team in New York and that you have these incredible talented players you're able to watch just in the back door and and in your city. And they are eventually going to move to at the end stadium, which is right across the street from City Field, and that's going to hold at least 25,000 seats. So, we know that, you know, in Queens there's going to be direct, you know, opportunity for about 3 million people to be able to, you know, at least go up when whenever they can to to watch the games. But it was an incredible scene. There were so many people who were just excited to be there to watch these these women do what they do best. And obviously Rose Lavelle scoring that goal just put a cherry on top of the night. So, incredibly evening. I'm so proud of them and hopefully this will continue. >> At what point did you stop and take a look around and think to yourself, this is more than just a regular season game? Did it feel like another turning point for the league? >> Yeah, it really felt like that because I was looking at the seats that they were, you know, people sitting in the very top of the stadium and that's just, you know, that's exactly what these women deserve, but we don't get that as often and especially not playing where they're playing now. It's it's a tough stadium to get to and so that's why they wanted to try to move closer to the city where there's, you know, more accessibility to get physically to get to the stadium for fans to be able to participate in such an incredible evening. And then that was just a proof of concept, so to speak, for for what's to come in the future. So, unbelievable scenes. The team won and hopefully it'll just continue. But that just shows the growth of women's sports now and I'm really excited to be a part of it. >> So, who's on your mind? Who you looking at in the NWSL now that the women are back from their break? >> Yeah, well, Lindsey Horan came back from her European years playing for Olympic Lyon and obviously won a Champions League there with them and had an incredible tenure there in Europe and now she's bringing her talents back to the NWSL, which is also going to get people to show up for Denver. She's originally from Denver and she's the captain of the national team. So, right before this year gearing up for the World Cup next summer, I think it's a great opportunity for her to really help with the foundation what Denver Summit is asking asking for and building a really great team there with, you know, such a good organization who are actually investing so much into the women. And it's just a really healthy opportunity for her and and she's going to really really do well there. And obviously, captain that team, lead that team to hopefully a lot of success in the future. >> And you mentioned next summer, so let's there right now. The Women's World Cup going to Brazil. It'll be the first Women's World Cup ever in South America. When you assess the team though, what is the biggest question that needs to be answered before next summer? >> Yeah, I mean, just every opportunity now, especially playing in these international games is going to be huge for the team. They're going to be gearing up against Spain come October, which is going to be a huge test for them. But these are the teams that you want to play against before such a big tournament because you want the opportunity to challenge yourself, to iron out those details, and iron out those, you know, mistakes that could potentially happen so that you're fully prepared for the real thing and the and the biggest tournament in the world. So you want to play against the top teams in the world. And and that one of them is definitely Spain. I think they're going to they're obviously, you know, won the World Cup last tournament, so, you know, they're reigning champions and they're going to be a difficult task. But these are the teams that we want to see the USWNT play against. They already played against Brazil in the Brazil in a tough environment and had a really difficult task at hand. They came through. They had lost one game, but then won the second game. So, these are great tests to have and I'm really excited to see what they can do this year gearing up for the biggest tournament in the world. >> That is a spicy rivalry, too, that they have with Brazil. I love watching those games. Oh my gosh. Um, but when you think about next year and this team, who do you think could become a potential household name who maybe isn't right now? Who's a little under the radar? >> Well, I think Lily Yohannes is such an incredibly young talent that we have. She plays alongside Lindsey Horan with Olympic Lyon and she's playing in Europe. But she is she's young. She's from Northern Virginia, which shout out to to Virginia. That's where I'm from as well in Springfield. So, she's, you know, has done so well in her young career already. She has so much experience. She's playing in midfield. She's creating chances. She's so smart um, and and knowledgeable about the game, which you don't see that always with a young talent like her. Um, she's going to be brilliant for the future of this team, and I know that they're going to be in great hands because because we have uh, staple players like like her and uh, representing the country on the world's biggest stage. Um, she's young, but she does have the potential to be one of the best midfielders that we've ever seen and produced in the United States. Um, it's going to be incredible to see what she can do. Uh, I'm really looking forward to that. And then obviously Sophia Wilson. And and also, you know, uh, you have Trinity Rodman, uh, you have Naomi Girma holding down the back line. These are These are such great players who we get to see week in and week out in the NWSL. >> There's some guys playing this weekend not anybody's really paying attention. So, before we let you go, really quick, who's going to win this? >> I think Spain is going to win. I think they've been, you know, building into the tournament uh, incredibly well. I think they have this possession you know, oriented style play. Uh, they have young talent. They're super skillful. Um, and they're showing uh, the complete performances with the complete team. So, I really believe that they're going to show up and show out. And it's going to be either way it's going to be a match up. And then you have Argentina who has Messi magic, right? And um, they've you know, slipped their way into the final and are obviously reigning champions. So, it's going to be a great battle. >> It's going to be a great one. We can't wait to watch it. We're so happy that you stopped by. Thank you so much for joining us and um, we'll talk to you soon, all right? Definitely before next year. >> Thank you. I'll definitely come back.
